{"summary":"Architecture memo (2026-08-07): Use GitHub App user access tokens obtained through device flow, not OAuth App tokens or pasted PATs, as the default. OAuth App `repo` scope includes private-repository write and broader organization capabilities, so it cannot enforce guest read-only access. A GitHub App token instead has the intersection of the app’s permissions, its installed repositories, and the user’s access.

Permission model: Preserve MSW’s server-enforced split with two distinct GitHub App registrations per workspace trust domain. The guest app requests only Metadata read and Contents read. The host app requests Metadata read and Contents read/write. Request no account or organization permissions and enable no webhooks. Do not grant Workflows by default; use a separate, explicit host-workflows app when workflow-file pushes are required. Install each app on selected repositories only. Separate registrations per dev/playgrounds/personal are necessary if their repository sets must remain isolated: one app installation has one repository selection per owner, while device-flow `repository_id` can restrict a user token to only one repository, not an arbitrary workspace set. Using just one global read/write app pair would collapse the existing per-workspace repository boundary.

OAuth flow: The menu app embeds only each GitHub App client ID, enables device flow in the app registrations, requests a device code from `https://github.com/login/device/code`, displays the user code, opens `https://github.com/login/device`, and polls `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` no faster than GitHub’s returned interval. Handle authorization_pending, slow_down, expiration, denial, cancellation, and account mismatch explicitly. Device flow requires no client secret, and refreshes of tokens originally obtained through device flow also omit the client secret. After authorization, verify the authenticated user and enumerate `/user/installations` plus each installation’s repositories before accepting the credential. Installation and user authorization are separate GitHub actions, so first-run must detect and guide both. Organization approval, SAML state, and enterprise policy can still block access.

Secret storage and rotation: Keep expiring user-token support enabled. Access tokens expire after eight hours and refresh tokens after six months. Store access and refresh tokens as separate macOS Keychain items protected by a signed-app/helper access group or designated-requirement ACL; do not expose refresh tokens to shell scripts, `security -w`, environment variables, argv, logs, defaults, crash reports, or backups. Store only non-secret app, account, installation, repository, permission, and expiry metadata in configuration files. Refresh ahead of expiry and atomically replace both returned tokens because using a refresh token immediately invalidates the prior refresh token and access token. If persistence or rebinding fails after refresh, the old pair cannot be restored: quarantine and stop that workspace, revoke host-write metadata, and require repair/reauthorization. On removal, first revoke metadata and quarantine locally, remove the guest binding, submit both `ghu_` and `ghr_` values to GitHub’s unauthenticated credential-revocation endpoint, then delete Keychain items. A 202 response is acceptance, not proof of immediate revocation; failed revocation must remain a recorded retry state rather than being reported as complete.

Guest injection: Bind only the read-app access token to MicroSandbox’s existing `GH_TOKEN@github.com,api.github.com` placeholder. Never bind the host-app token. The current clone/pull and negative push test remain valuable because GitHub, not a local hook, must reject guest writes. Refresh introduces a new constraint: the repository does not demonstrate an atomic live replacement of a bound secret. Until that is proven, rotate under the existing lock and quarantine, rebind/restart, verify read access and guest-push rejection, then clear quarantine. A dynamic signed host token broker could avoid storing an access token in broadly readable generic-password items, but its exact integration with MicroSandbox secret substitution must be proven before making a stronger claim.

Push design: Retain `push_impl`’s verified current-branch Git bundle, exact commit comparison, isolated temporary HOME, empty environment, disabled global/system Git configuration and hooks, no SSH agent, fast-forward default, exact force-with-lease, and SHA-256-verified LFS transfer. The native UI should display workspace, canonical repository, path, branch, commit, mode, and outgoing commits, then require an explicit confirmation; biometric/user-presence protection for releasing the host credential is appropriate. A signed XPC/token broker or tightly ACLed signed askpass helper should supply the refreshed host token to Git over an anonymous pipe, never argv or the guest. The server-side app installation remains the definitive push allowlist. Keep the temporary-branch verification and cleanup transaction.

Quarantine and migration: Preserve the current ordering in `bin/msw`: acquire the per-workspace lock, arm interruption handling, create and prove quarantine before credential mutation, revoke metadata before fallible cleanup, verify in a fresh process, and clear quarantine only after success or a completely successful rollback. During PAT-to-App migration, retain the previous PAT configuration until the staged App tokens pass guest-read, guest-push-rejection, host-push, confirmation, and cleanup checks. Only then revoke/delete the PATs. Pre-existing quarantined workspaces must never treat their old credentials as trusted rollback state.

Required CLI changes: Replace `read_hidden_token` and normal `msw github setup` token-paste inputs with non-secret IPC from the native app; retain PAT entry only as an explicitly labeled legacy/admin fallback. Version the credential metadata and distinguish read/write access tokens, refresh tokens, expiry, app identity, GitHub account, installations, and verified repository set. Route `start_sandbox`, restart, SSH proxy startup, setup-time rebinding, `bind_github_read_token`, verification, and host askpass through the signed broker so each operation receives a valid refreshed token. Update status to report app identity, account, expiration/reauthorization, installation drift, access mode, and quarantine without revealing credentials. Update remove to perform remote revocation and pending-retry handling. Preserve `host_git_run` isolation and metadata authorization. Add focused tests for device-flow polling/error states, account mismatch, refresh success and one-time invalidation, Keychain write failure after refresh, repository/permission drift, app-pair workspace separation, revocation failure, migration rollback, no secret leakage, and interruption/quarantine behavior. Existing boundary tests in `tests/test_suite.py` should remain.

Distribution assumptions: A genuinely no-terminal first run requires a new Developer-ID-signed, notarized, hardened-runtime menu-bar app plus signed helper(s), packaged dependencies, signed updates, and an Authorization Services/privileged-helper path for host networking changes. The current `setup.sh` installs through Homebrew, edits shell profiles, and reaches an interactive `sudo` boundary; the documented macOS canary stopped there. Therefore the current repository cannot truthfully claim no-terminal first run. No-terminal also cannot mean zero interaction: GitHub installation/authorization, organization approval, and macOS administrator consent remain unavoidable. Shipping a GitHub App client ID is acceptable; shipping a client secret or App private key is not. Installation access tokens could be narrowed to selected repositories and reduced permissions for one hour, but minting them requires a JWT signed by the App private key. That demands a trusted backend or locally provisioned high-value private key and is not recommended for this standalone desktop design.

Exact limitations: A single write-capable GitHub App user token cannot be made read-only with OAuth scopes because GitHub App user tokens have an empty scope and fixed app permissions. One global app pair cannot preserve arbitrary multi-repository per-workspace selections under the same owner. A backend-free native app cannot safely mint installation tokens. Read-only GitHub credentials do not prevent an internet-enabled guest from exfiltrating readable files elsewhere, isolate repositories inside one workspace, or protect against compromise of the signed host app or macOS user account. Repository rules, app-installation changes, SAML, enterprise restrictions, and workflow permission requirements may reject otherwise authorized operations. Public repositories remain publicly readable. Device-flow access requires periodic refresh and reauthorization after six months offline. These constraints prohibit claims of zero-touch setup, universal organization compatibility, perfect secret non-extractability, or data-loss prevention.

Evidence: Current behavior was inspected in `docs/GITHUB-SETUP.md`, `bin/msw`, and `tests/test_suite.py`, including Keychain separation, host-only askpass, guest binding, verification branches, locks, quarantine, rollback, read-only metadata, bundle/LFS controls, and simulated failure tests. Official GitHub evidence: user-token permissions/device flow and single-repository restriction: https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-a-user-access-token-for-a-github-app ; App Git permissions: https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/registering-a-github-app/choosing-permissions-for-a-github-app ; refresh lifetimes and device-flow secret exception: https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/refreshing-user-access-tokens ; installation selection: https://docs.github.com/en/apps/using-github-apps/installing-a-github-app-from-a-third-party ; OAuth `repo` scope breadth: https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/scopes-for-oauth-apps ; installation-token narrowing and one-hour lifetime: https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-an-installation-access-token-for-a-github-app ; private-key requirement: https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/managing-private-keys-for-github-apps ; credential revocation: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/credentials/revoke . Verification was read-only: no tests, linters, formatters, or repository files were changed; the pre-existing dirty worktree remained unchanged.","filesChanged":[]}
